entry: Landlocked state in the western United States. Utah is one of the Four Corners states, bordering [[Arizona]], [[Colorado]] and [[New Mexico]]. Its population is just over three million. Most residents live along the Wasatch Front, which includes the capital, [[Salt Lake City]]. Part of New Spain and later Mexico, the region was annexed by the [[United States]] in 1848, after the [[Mexican–American War]]. Utah was admitted as the 45th state in 1896, after agreeing to outlaw [[Polygamy|polygamy]]. Slightly over half of Utahns are Mormons, most of them members of [[The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]].

Organ of the female reproductive system in most [[Mammal|mammals]], including humans, in which one or more fertilized eggs develop until birth. The uterus is a hormone-responsive sex organ whose lining contains glands that secrete uterine milk to nourish the embryo. A fertilized egg travels along the fallopian tube and implants in the endometrium, where it develops into an [[Embryo|embryo]] and later a [[Fetus|fetus]]. In humans the uterus lies in the [[Pelvis|pelvis]] behind the [[Bladder|bladder]] and in front of the sigmoid colon. It is pear-shaped and about 7.6 cm (3.0 in) long, and a typical adult uterus weighs about 60 grams. The uterus has three layers: the endometrium, the myometrium and the perimetrium. Ligaments hold it in position within the pelvis. The functional layer of the endometrium thickens and is shed during the menstrual cycle, and the uterus expands dramatically during [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. In medicine the term uterus is standard, while womb is the everyday word.

Third Rashidun caliph, reigning 644–656. Uthman was a second cousin, son-in-law and senior companion of the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]]. He was chosen as successor by a council of six companions appointed by [[Umar]], and at his accession he was the oldest person to become caliph. His reign saw the caliphate expand into Persia, reaching [[Khorasan]] and Transoxiana in the east and Ifriqiya and the Iberian Peninsula in the west. He introduced centralized administrative reforms and fostered rapid economic growth. His most lasting achievement was the standardized Quran, the Uthmanic codex, which established the uniform written text used by [[Muslims]] today. Discontent over his fiscal policies and the appointment of relatives to key positions grew in his final years. Rebels besieged his residence in [[Medina]] and assassinated him in 656, an event that contributed to later political and sectarian conflicts. Sunni tradition regards him as the third rightly guided caliph.

Family of theories in normative ethics that prescribe actions maximizing happiness and well-being. It is a version of [[Consequentialism|consequentialism]], which holds that the consequences of an action alone determine whether it is right or wrong. Utilitarian ideas aim at the greatest good for the greatest number. [[Jeremy Bentham]] founded the modern tradition, describing utility as the capacity of actions to produce pleasure and happiness or to prevent pain. [[John Stuart Mill]] later distinguished higher intellectual pleasures from lower sensual ones. Proponents disagree on whether to judge individual acts by their likely results (act utilitarianism) or to follow rules that maximize utility (rule utilitarianism), and on whether total or average utility should be maximized. The theory has influenced cost-benefit analysis in economics and reforms in law and animal welfare. Critics argue that it can justify violating individual rights when the net gain in utility is large, and that utility is difficult to measure and compare across individuals.

Family of Native American languages found almost entirely in the western United States and [[Mexico]]. The name reflects the common ancestry of the Ute language of [[Utah]] and the Nahuan languages, also called Aztecan, of Mexico. Ethnologue gives 61 languages and 1,900,412 speakers in total, and speakers of Nahuatl languages account for over 85% of these. The family is usually divided into a northern branch, covering the languages of the United States, and a southern branch, covering those of Mexico. Numic, including Comanche and Shoshoni, and Takic are the main northern groups. Southern groups include Tepiman, Tarahumaran, Cahitan, Corachol and Nahuan. The homeland is generally thought to lie in the Southwestern United States or northwestern Mexico. The Aztec script, the best-known [[Pre-Columbian era|pre-Columbian]] [[Writing system|writing system]] of the family, combined ideographic writing with phonetic and syllabic signs.

Imagined community or society with highly desirable or near-perfect qualities for its residents. [[Thomas More]] coined the term in 1516 for his book [[Utopia (book)|Utopia]], which describes a fictional island society. The word comes from Greek for "no place," but More noted its similarity to eutopia, "good place," and the two are pronounced alike, which may have caused the shift in meaning. In standard usage it now describes a nonexistent society meant to be seen as far better than contemporary society. Hypothetical utopias focus on equality in economics, government and justice, and proposed methods vary with ideology. Lyman Tower Sargent argues that utopias are inherently contradictory, because societies contain conflicting desires. The opposite of a utopia is a dystopia, which surpassed utopia in popularity in fiction from the 1950s onward, chiefly because of George Orwell's [[Nineteen Eighty-Four]].

Work of fiction and socio-political satire by [[Thomas More]], written in Latin. It was published in 1516 and revised in 1518. Its frame narrative depicts a fictional island society and its religious, social and political customs, and many aspects of the island are reminiscent of life in monasteries. The title translates roughly as "Of a republic's best state and of the new island Utopia." The name derives from Greek roots meaning "no place," which emphasizes its fictionality. The first book is a dialogue set in [[Antwerp]], in which the traveler Raphael Hythlodaeus criticizes European rulers for starting wars and for punishing theft with execution. He blames most theft on [[Enclosure|enclosure]]. Other sections describe Utopia itself, where property is communally owned and labor is limited to six hours daily. Scholars continue to debate whether More endorsed this vision or used it to show the impracticality of such schemes.

State in northern India, with over 241 million inhabitants, the most populous state in the country. Its capital is [[Lucknow]], and [[Prayagraj]] is the judicial capital. The state covers 243,286 km2 (93,933 sq mi), the fourth-largest Indian state by area. It was established in 1950, after India became a republic, as successor to the United Provinces. Most of the state lies on the [[Indo-Gangetic Plain]], and the Ganges and its tributary, the [[Yamuna]], meet at the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj. Hindi is the official language, with Urdu as an additional official language. The region formed part of the territories of the Maurya, Gupta and Mughal empires, among others. It played a central role in the Indian independence movement, including the [[Indian Rebellion of 1857]]. Its economy is now dominated by services, and it contains Hindu pilgrimage sites such as [[Varanasi]] and the Taj Mahal.

State in northern India, bordered by [[Tibet]] to the north and [[Nepal]] to the east. Known as Uttaranchal until 2007, it covers 53,483 km2 (20,650 sq mi). Its name means "Northern Land." Dehradun is the winter capital, and Nainital is the judicial capital. The [[Ganges]] and [[Yamuna]] rivers rise in the Gangotri and Yamunotri glaciers. Forest covers 45.4% of the state. Hinduism is practiced by more than three-fourths of the population, and the state is known as Devabhumi, "Land of the Gods," for its many temples and pilgrimage centers, including Haridwar and Rishikesh. Agriculture and hydropower were long primary, but the service industry now dominates the economy.

Turkic empire in East Asia, self-described as the Toquz Oghuz ("Nine Tribes"), that existed from 744 to 840. It was a tribal confederation under the Uyghur nobility, and Kutlug I Bilge Khagan built its capital at Ordu-Baliq. In 745 the Uyghurs killed the last khagan of the [[Göktürks]]. Under Bayanchur Khan the empire expanded rapidly, bringing many steppe peoples under its rule and using profits from trading outposts with the [[Tang dynasty]] to build cities. In 757 about 4,000 Uyghur horsemen helped Tang armies retake Chang'an and [[Luoyang]]. Bögü Qaghan made [[Manichaeism]] the state religion in 762. Its economy relied on [[Silk Road]] trade in furs, horses and luxury goods. The khaganate declined through factionalism and fiscal strain, and a Kyrgyz invasion destroyed it in 840.

Turkic ethnic group of Central and East Asia, and the titular nationality of Xinjiang in northwestern China. They speak Uyghur, a Karluk language closely related to Uzbek, and are one of China's 55 officially recognized ethnic minorities. Most were converted to [[Islam]] after the 10th century, and by the 16th century most identified as Muslims. The name "Uyghur" was not used as a common ethnonym until the 20th century, when Turkic intellectuals gathered in [[Tashkent]] and adopted it, although the medieval [[Uyghur Khaganate]] did not cover the whole area of modern Uyghur settlement. More Uyghurs live in the Tarim Basin than in northern Xinjiang. Communities also live in [[Kazakhstan]], [[Kyrgyzstan]], [[Uzbekistan]] and [[Turkey]]. Since 2014 the Chinese government has been accused of widespread persecution of Uyghurs, including arbitrary detention, forced sterilization and forced labor. The Chinese government denies the accusations.

Karluk Turkic language, the official and national language of [[Uzbekistan]]. It succeeded Chagatai, an earlier Karluk literary language, as the literary language of Uzbekistan in the 1920s. Ethnologue counts more than 36 million native speakers, making Uzbek the second-most widely spoken Turkic language after Turkish. Northern Uzbek is spoken in Uzbekistan, neighboring Central Asian countries and China, while Southern Uzbek is spoken in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Uzbek is the western member of the Karluk branch, whose eastern member is [[Uyghurs|Uyghur]]. Persian influence has almost completely eliminated vowel harmony from Standard Uzbek, and the language has borrowed heavily from Persian, Russian and Arabic. In 2021 the government announced a plan to switch fully from [[Cyrillic script|Cyrillic]] to the Latin alphabet by January 1, 2023, a deadline later extended several times. As of 2024, most institutions still use both alphabets.

Doubly landlocked country in Central Asia, bordered by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan. Its population of more than 39 million makes it the most populous country in Central Asia, and [[Tashkent]] is its capital. Uzbek is the official language, while Russian serves as a lingua franca. The area was home to [[Scythians|Scythian]] kingdoms and later formed part of the Achaemenid and Sasanian empires, until the Muslim conquest of Persia. The early Muslim conquests and the Samanid Empire spread Islam, and cities grew rich on the [[Silk Road]]. In the 14th century [[Timur]] established the [[Timurid Empire]], whose capital, [[Samarkand]], became a center of science under Ulugh Beg. Most of Central Asia was incorporated into the [[Russian Empire]] in the 19th century. In 1924 the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic was created, and Uzbekistan declared independence in 1991 after the Soviet collapse. The country is a secular state and a major producer and exporter of [[Cotton|cotton]].

Discontinued standard for consumer analog video recording on [[Magnetic tape|magnetic tape]] cassettes. Introduced on September 9, 1976, by the Victor Company of Japan (JVC), it won the format war against [[Sony]]'s Betamax and became the dominant home video format of the 1980s and 1990s, aided by the video rental market. Its 0.5-inch (12.7 mm) tape typically offered at least two hours of recording. Its popularity peaked in the late 1990s and then declined after the introduction of [[DVD]], and VHS rentals were surpassed by DVD in the United States in 2003. Production of all VHS equipment ceased by 2016, although collectors keep the format alive.

Free, open-source, cross-platform media player and streaming media server developed by the VideoLAN project. It runs on desktop systems such as [[Linux]], [[MacOS|macOS]] and Windows, and on mobile platforms including [[Android (operating system)|Android]] and [[IOS|iOS]]. It supports many compression methods and file formats, including DVD-Video, can stream media over computer networks and can transcode files. Its default distribution includes free decoding libraries, so users rarely need proprietary plugins. The project began in 1996 as a French academic project, and version 1.0.0 was released on July 7, 2009.

German long-range ballistic missile of World War II, also known as Aggregat-4 (A4). Developed in [[Nazi Germany]] as a "vengeance weapon," it was the world's first practical modern ballistic missile. Beginning in September 1944, more than 3,000 V-2s were launched against Allied targets, mainly [[London]] and [[Antwerp]]. A 2011 BBC documentary estimates that the attacks killed 9,000 civilians and military personnel, while 12,000 laborers and concentration camp prisoners died producing the missiles. Although the rockets had little strategic impact, they strongly influenced later rocketry. Through [[Operation Paperclip]], the United States acquired captured hardware and personnel.

Vietnamese general and communist politician who led the Việt Minh and the People's Army of Vietnam in the Indochina wars. A former history teacher with no formal military training before World War II, he became military commander of the Việt Minh in 1941. He won a decisive victory at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, which ended the [[First Indochina War]]. He commanded during the [[Tet Offensive]] of 1968 and the 1972 Easter Offensive. Giáp was the principal architect of the [[Ho Chi Minh]] trail, a logistics network through Laos and Cambodia. He served as defense minister of North Vietnam and later of unified Vietnam until 1980, and he oversaw the 1978 invasion of Cambodia. Giáp is widely regarded as a gifted military leader, although some assessments emphasize the heavy losses his strategies accepted among his own troops.

[[Trinidad and Tobago]]-born British writer of fiction and nonfiction in English. Naipaul won a government scholarship and studied English at [[Oxford]]. His early comic novels were set in Trinidad, and his breakthrough novel, *A House for Mr Biswas* (1961), drew on his father's life. Later works portrayed alienation and post-colonial disorder in the wider world, while his travel writing covered [[India]] and Islamic societies. He won the [[Booker Prize]] in 1971 for *In a Free State*, and the 2001 Nobel Prize in Literature, awarded "for having united perceptive narrative and incorruptible scrutiny in works that compel us to see the presence of suppressed histories." He published more than thirty books. His skeptical views on post-colonial nationalism and Islam drew criticism, and some critics charged him with cultural bias. He was knighted in 1990.

Czech playwright, dissident and statesman, last president of Czechoslovakia (1989–1992) and first president of the Czech Republic (1993–2003). His absurdist plays, such as *The Garden Party* and *The Memorandum*, criticized the communist system. After taking part in the [[Prague Spring]] and being blacklisted after the [[Warsaw Pact]] invasion, he helped found dissident groups, including Charter 77. He was imprisoned several times, the longest term lasting nearly four years, from 1979 to 1983. His Civic Forum party played a major role in the 1989 Velvet Revolution that toppled communist rule. As president, he was instrumental in dismantling the Warsaw Pact and in the eastward enlargement of [[NATO]]. His opposition to Slovak independence and his general amnesty for those imprisoned under communism were controversial. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and the international airport in [[Prague]] was renamed for him in 2012.

Dystopian graphic novel by [[Alan Moore]] and David Lloyd. Set in a 1990s Britain after a nuclear war, under the fascist Norsefire party, it follows V, an anarchist who wears a [[Guy Fawkes]] mask and wages a theatrical campaign against the regime while mentoring Evey Hammond. Serialized in black and white in the British anthology *Warrior* from 1982 to 1985, it was completed in a ten-issue color series by [[DC Comics]] in 1988 and 1989. A 2005 film adaptation was written by the [[The Wachowskis|Wachowski siblings]]. Moore disavowed the film and asked for his name to be removed from it.

Largest lake in Sweden and the largest in the European Union, and the third-largest lake in Europe after [[Lake Ladoga|Ladoga]] and [[Lake Onega|Onega]] in Russia. It lies in the provinces of Västergötland, Dalsland and Värmland in southwestern Sweden. The lake covers 5,655 km2 (2,183 sq mi), about twice the area of [[Luxembourg]]. Its surface is 44 m (144 ft) above sea level, and its maximum depth is 106 m (348 ft), though its average depth is 27 m (89 ft). Vänern drains through the Göta älv toward [[Gothenburg]] and the [[Kattegat]]. Its main tributary, the Klarälven, enters near Karlstad. The lake's water level is regulated by the Vargön Hydroelectric Power Station. Its archipelago contains about 22,000 islands, islets and skerries, and the area is part of a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

Leave of absence from work or school, or leisure travel away from home. In British English the same break is called a holiday. Travel for recreation was once a luxury of the wealthy, as on the Grand Tour, and the modern concept developed over the last two centuries. Paid vacations spread in Europe in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as labor laws mandated holiday entitlement for workers. Mass tourism, enabled by railways and later commercial aviation, made travel accessible to more people. Statutory entitlements differ widely: France and Germany mandate around 30 days, while the United States has no federal minimum and workers take an average of 11–14 days a year. Research on the effects of vacations on health and work performance began in the 1990s.

Administration of a [[Vaccine|vaccine]] to help the immune system develop immunity to a disease. Vaccines contain a microorganism or virus in a weakened or killed state, or proteins or toxins from it. When a sufficiently large share of a population is vaccinated, herd immunity results, protecting people who cannot be vaccinated. Vaccination is the most effective method of preventing infectious disease, and it was largely responsible for the worldwide eradication of [[Smallpox|smallpox]] and the elimination of [[Polio|polio]] and [[Tetanus|tetanus]] from much of the world. The [[World Health Organization]] estimates that vaccination prevents 3.5–5 million deaths per year. The smallpox vaccine was invented in 1796 by [[Edward Jenner]], and [[Louis Pasteur]] furthered the concept through his work in microbiology. Smallpox was eradicated in 1979.

Delay in accepting, or refusal of, vaccines despite their availability and supporting evidence. Causes include a lack of scientific knowledge, fear of needles, distrust of public authorities or of the vaccine itself, complacency and inconvenience. Although adverse effects are occasionally observed, the scientific consensus that vaccines are generally safe and effective is overwhelming. Hesitancy often results in outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases, and the [[World Health Organization]] characterizes it as one of the top ten global health threats. Myths and misinformation spread by anti-vaccination movements fuel it. Opposition to mandatory vaccination may reflect concern about civil liberties, distrust of the pharmaceutical industry or suspicion of profiteering. When diseases become rare, people may underestimate their danger, which reduces the perceived benefit of [[Vaccine|vaccination]].

Membrane-bound organelle present in plant, fungal and some protist, animal and bacterial cells. Vacuoles are compartments filled with water containing inorganic and organic molecules, including [[Enzyme|enzymes]], and sometimes engulfed solids. They form by the fusion of membrane vesicles and have no fixed shape or size. [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]] described the plant vacuole in 1676. In plant cells the vacuole stores water and maintains turgor pressure, which supports leaves and flowers. Vacuoles also contain waste, maintain an acidic internal pH and export unwanted substances. In seeds, protein-storage vacuoles hold proteins needed for germination. In protists they store absorbed food. In animal cells vacuoles are smaller and more numerous, and they mainly assist exocytosis and endocytosis.
